lesson.title: Undercoverage: The People Who Never Had a Chance
lesson.summary: Undercoverage occurs when some members of the population have no chance, or a much smaller chance, of being selected for the sample at all, biasing results before a single response is even collected.
lesson.body:
Every sampling method starts from some list, frame, or accessible portion of the population from which the sample is actually drawn, and undercoverage happens whenever that starting point leaves out part of the population entirely, or gives it a much smaller chance of inclusion than the rest. This is a flaw in the sampling frame itself, the list or mechanism used to reach people, rather than a flaw in how the sample is drawn from that frame. Even a perfectly executed simple random sample, one where every name on the list truly has an equal chance of selection, produces a biased result if the list never contained certain kinds of people in the first place.

A classic illustration involves phone surveys conducted only by calling landline numbers. Even if the interviewer dials landline numbers using a flawless random-digit process, anyone who only owns a cell phone, a group that skews younger, is simply not reachable through that frame and has zero chance of appearing in the sample no matter how the randomization is done. The randomization inside the frame was flawless; the frame itself failed to cover part of the population. This distinguishes undercoverage from the earlier sampling errors discussed in this course: convenience and voluntary response samples are non-random by design, while undercoverage can occur even within an otherwise properly randomized sample, because the damage happens at the frame-building stage, before randomization ever begins.

Consider a hypothetical example. A university wants to survey its 12,000 undergraduates about satisfaction with campus dining by randomly sampling 500 names from the student email directory. If 300 students never activated a university email account and communicate only through personal addresses the registrar does not have on file, those 300 students have no chance whatsoever of being drawn into the sample, regardless of how carefully the random selection among the other 11,700 names is carried out. If those 300 students differ systematically from the rest, perhaps they are disproportionately students who disengaged from campus life partly because of dining hall problems, the survey's dining satisfaction estimate would be biased upward, missing exactly the complaints it most needed to capture.

Undercoverage connects directly back to the definition of a population, the complete group a study intends to describe. Whenever the group actually accessible through the sampling frame is smaller than, or systematically different from, the intended population, the resulting sample describes the frame, not the population the researcher claims to be studying. Fixing undercoverage requires improving the frame itself, adding a mixed-mode option such as mail or in-person contact alongside phone or email, rather than adjusting how randomly the existing frame is sampled, since no amount of careful randomization among the covered part of the population can reach the people the frame never included.

Undercoverage is often subtle because a sample can look perfectly sized and perfectly randomized on paper while still quietly excluding a meaningful slice of the population through its frame. Recognizing undercoverage requires asking a question that comes before any statistical calculation: who had a chance of being selected in the first place, and does that group actually match the population the study claims to describe? When the answer is no, the sample's random selection process, however well executed, cannot repair the gap.
